questions.lead: A new business location with employees (a shop, a branch, an office) opens in the US.
questions.ask: What percent of new locations like it are still open ten years later?
questions.fact: BLS follows every new private-sector business location. Ten years on, between 32.4% and 33.8% were still open in the cohorts it reports (33.6% of those that opened in the year to March 1994, 32.8% of those in the year to March 2006).
questions.why: Business survival is a slow leak, not a cliff: about two in three new businesses are gone within a decade. The longer the horizon, the more the odds favour closure.
questions.src_name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Business Employment Dynamics

questions.lead: The first round of the men's NCAA basketball tournament: a 3 seed plays a 14 seed. Think of every such game since 1985 (164 of them through 2026).
questions.ask: What percent of those games did the 14 seed win?
questions.fact: Since 1985 a 14 seed has beaten a 3 seed in 23 of 164 first-round games (14.02%).
questions.why: A 14 seed wins about one game in seven. 'Anything can happen' is true in March, but not everything is equally likely.
questions.src_name: Wikipedia: NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament upsets

questions.lead: A company files a new drug with the FDA for approval.
questions.ask: What percent of filings like it are approved?
questions.fact: BIO's data for 2011 to 2020 (1,453 filings): 90.6% of new drug filings were approved, counting re-submissions.
questions.why: Once a drug has cleared its big trials and the filing is in, approval is the usual outcome. Judge a late-stage event differently from an early one.
questions.src_name: BIO, Informa Pharma Intelligence and QLS: Clinical Development Success Rates 2011-2020

questions.lead: A student starts a certificate or associate degree full-time at a US two-year college in fall 2017.
questions.ask: What percent of students like them finish within one and a half times the normal length?
questions.fact: NCES reports that about 34% of first-time, full-time students who started a certificate or associate degree at a US two-year college in fall 2017 finished within 150% of the normal time.
questions.why: Plans meet reality: only about one student in three finishes a short course, a certificate or a two-year degree, within one and a half times the planned time.
questions.src_name: US National Center for Education Statistics: Undergraduate graduation rates

questions.lead: A student starts a bachelor's degree full-time at a US four-year college in fall 2014.
questions.ask: What percent of students like them graduate from that college within six years?
questions.fact: NCES reports that 64% of first-time, full-time students who started a bachelor's degree at a US four-year college in fall 2014 had graduated within six years.
questions.why: Finishing a degree is likelier than not but far from automatic: roughly a third of the students who start a bachelor's degree have not graduated from that college six years later.
questions.src_name: US National Center for Education Statistics: Undergraduate graduation rates

questions.lead: A megaproject (a rail line, an airport, a tunnel, a dam, anything costing over a billion dollars) is approved with a budget.
questions.ask: What percent of projects like it end up over budget?
questions.fact: Bent Flyvbjerg's research on megaprojects (those costing over a billion dollars): 'Nine out of ten megaprojects have cost overruns.'
questions.why: Over budget is the rule for giant projects, not the exception. Treat 'on budget' as the claim that needs evidence.
questions.src_name: Flyvbjerg (2014): What You Should Know About Megaprojects and Why, Project Management Institute

questions.lead: A drug candidate starts its first trial in people (Phase I).
questions.ask: What percent of candidates like it eventually win FDA approval?
questions.fact: Industry data on 12,728 drug programmes (BIO, Informa and QLS, 2011 to 2020): 7.9% of the programmes that entered Phase I were eventually approved.
questions.why: The drug pipeline is a funnel with a narrow end: most candidates fail somewhere along the way, however good the early news. A promising first trial is a weak signal of an eventual medicine.
questions.src_name: BIO, Informa Pharma Intelligence and QLS: Clinical Development Success Rates 2011-2020

questions.lead: A new business location with employees (a shop, a branch, an office) opens in the US.
questions.ask: What percent of new locations like it are still open a year later?
questions.fact: BLS follows every new private-sector business location. A year after opening, between 75.7% and 79.9% were still open in the cohorts it reports (79.6% of those that opened in the year to March 1994, 78.3% of those in the year to March 2006).
questions.why: Most new businesses survive their first year, and the failures people remember are the minority. Start from how often cases like this one survive, then adjust for what you know about this one.
questions.src_name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Business Employment Dynamics

questions.lead: A city wins the right to host an Olympic Games and sets a budget.
questions.ask: What percent of Games like it ended up costing more than budgeted?
questions.fact: In the Oxford Olympics Study every one of the 19 Games with data, from 1960 to 2016, ran over budget in real terms: 'cost overrun is found in all Games, without exception'.
questions.why: Budgets for one-off mega-events are set before the hard problems appear. When a budget is the only estimate, the outside view says expect it to rise.
questions.src_name: Flyvbjerg, Stewart and Budzier: The Oxford Olympics Study 2016

questions.lead: Someone in the US is diagnosed with cancer, of any type.
questions.ask: What percent of people like them are still alive five years later?
questions.fact: The US National Cancer Institute's SEER programme reports a five-year relative survival of 70.5% for all cancers combined (2016 to 2022).
questions.why: More people than not survive cancer for five years, though the odds vary enormously by cancer type and stage. One headline number hides very different cases.

questions.lead: A US adult is asked, in a Federal Reserve survey in October 2025, whether they could pay a surprise $400 expense with cash or its equivalent.

questions.fact: In the Federal Reserve's survey of October 2025, 63% of US adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent. The figure was the same in each of the previous three years and 68% in 2021.

questions.why: The favourite is nearly certain to win but not certain. A near-certain event still deserves a little doubt: 99 in 100 is not 100 in 100.

questions.src_name: BIO, Informa Pharma Intelligence and QLS: Clinical Development Success Rates 2011-2020

questions.lead: A drug candidate is in its Phase II trial, the first real test of whether it works.
